title: Poisson Process: Counts, Inter-arrival Times and Waiting Times
breadcrumb: Stochastic processes → Poisson process → Counts and waiting times
engineName: Translate between event counts, inter-arrival times and waiting-time distributions using the rate λ.
objectives: Recognise the defining assumptions and rate parameter of a homogeneous Poisson process.
Calculate event-count probabilities using N(t) ~ Poisson(λt).
Derive and use exponential inter-arrival and waiting-time distributions.
Find the distribution and moments of the time to the kth event.
Use independent and stationary increments and the exponential memoryless property without confusing counts with waiting times.

prereq.name: Poisson distribution
prereq.why: The number of events in an interval of length t has a Poisson distribution with mean λt.

prereq.name: Exponential distribution
prereq.why: The time between successive events has an exponential distribution with rate λ.

prereq.name: Integration and factorials
prereq.why: Waiting-time probabilities and Poisson count probabilities require these calculations.

traps: λ is a rate per unit time; λt is the expected count over an interval of length t.
Use the same time unit for λ and t.
P(N(t)=n) is a count probability; P(T₁>t) is a waiting-time survival probability.
The inter-arrival time is exponential with mean 1/λ, not λ.
The time to the kth event is Gamma/Erlang, not exponential when k>1.
Independent increments apply to disjoint intervals; stationary increments depend only on interval length.
At an arbitrary time, the residual waiting time is exponential by memorylessness; this is not a claim that all conditional waiting questions are identical.
howto: Start by identifying whether the question asks for a count, the first waiting time, an inter-arrival time or the kth arrival time. Convert the rate to the stated time unit. Write the distribution before substituting numbers, then check units and whether the event is 'by t', 'after t' or 'exactly n'.

The v4.1 revision expands foundation rebuilds, adds a transfer exercise on the third arrival, a concise summary and a mastery test; the original scenario and numerical examples remain intact.

sheet: A homogeneous Poisson process has rate λ>0 and N(0)=0.
Counts on disjoint intervals are independent; increment distributions depend only on interval length.
Inter-arrival times X₁,X₂,… are iid Exp(λ).
Time T_k to the kth event has Gamma/Erlang(k, rate λ) distribution.
Use consistent time units and distinguish exactly n, at least n and no events.
cards: Expected number of events per unit time.
T_k is Gamma/Erlang with shape k and rate λ.
Counts in disjoint time intervals are independent.
A count over an interval depends on its length, not its location.
tricks: If the rate is r per hour and time is in minutes, use λ=r/60 per minute or convert minutes to hours.
'Wait more than t' is e^(−λt); 'arrive by t' is 1−e^(−λt).
For the kth event, use the Erlang survival/CDF or the equivalent Poisson-count identity.
shortcuts: Coefficient of variation of an exponential waiting time is 1.
remember: Poisson counts and exponential gaps are two descriptions of the same homogeneous process.
Independent increments do not mean event counts at overlapping intervals are independent.
The sum of k iid Exp(λ) inter-arrival times is Gamma(k,λ).

scenes.title: Refresh rates, counts and exponentials
scenes.objective: Rebuild the probability tools needed for the Poisson process.
body: A rate describes an average number of events per unit time. If calls arrive at an average rate of 6 per hour, the expected number in 30 minutes is 6×(1/2)=3.
A Poisson random variable models a nonnegative integer count. An exponential random variable models a nonnegative waiting time. They are related, but they are not the same random variable.
For an exponential variable with rate λ, the survival probability is e^(−λt), the mean is 1/λ and the variance is 1/λ². The parameter is a rate, so its reciprocal has time units.

items.ask: If events occur at 8 per hour, what is the expected count in 15 minutes?
refresh: A rate λ is measured in events per unit time. To find the expected count in a time interval, multiply the rate by the interval length after converting both to compatible units.
With 8 events per hour and a 15-minute interval, first write 15 minutes as one quarter of an hour. The expected count is therefore 8×(1/4)=2 events.
An expected count is an average over repeated intervals. It can be non-integer even though each observed count is a whole number; the Poisson distribution describes the variation around that mean.
The exponential distribution models a nonnegative waiting time. Its cumulative distribution function is F(t)=1−e^(−λt), for t≥0, so the probability of waiting longer than t is the complement.
Subtract the CDF from one: P(X>t)=1−F(t)=1−(1−e^(−λt))=e^(−λt). This is the survival probability, not the probability of an arrival by time t.
Use the wording carefully: 'more than t' uses e^(−λt), while 'within t' uses 1−e^(−λt). The product λt must be dimensionless, so rate and time units must match.

items.ask: If X~Exp(λ), what is its mean?
refresh: For an exponential waiting time with rate λ, the density is f(t)=λe^(−λt), t≥0. Integrating t f(t) gives the mean waiting time 1/λ; a larger rate therefore means a shorter average wait.
The rate λ is not itself the mean. If λ=4 events per hour, the mean waiting time is 1/4 hour, or 15 minutes. Always state the reciprocal in time units.
The variance is 1/λ², measured in squared time units. A useful dimensional check is that a rate has units 1/time, so its reciprocal is a time and its reciprocal square is time squared.

ask.q: Which distribution describes a count, and which describes a waiting time?

scenes.title: Events arriving over time
scenes.objective: Interpret a homogeneous Poisson process in a practical setting.
body: Imagine a help desk receiving independent incoming calls at a stable average rate. The process records how many calls have arrived by time t.
A homogeneous Poisson process assumes a constant rate over time and independent counts in disjoint time intervals. Its count distribution depends on the interval length.
The model does not say that calls arrive at perfectly regular intervals. Short gaps and long gaps both occur; the exponential distribution describes the gaps.

scenario.title: Calls during a shift
body: A support desk receives calls at an average rate of 4 per hour. The model treats arrivals as a homogeneous Poisson process: the rate is stable during the period considered, and arrivals in disjoint intervals are independent.

The supervisor asks two different questions. First: how many calls arrive in the next half-hour? This is a count question. Second: how long until the next call? This is a waiting-time question. Both use λ=4 per hour, but their probability distributions are different.
Over half an hour the Poisson mean is λt=2. The time to the next call is exponential with rate 4 per hour and mean 1/4 hour, or 15 minutes.
scenario.q: What is the expected number of calls in 30 minutes, and what is the mean wait for the next call?
scenario.answer: Expected count = 4×0.5=2 calls. Mean wait = 1/4 hour = 15 minutes.

ask.q: Why do the count and waiting-time questions use different distributions?
ask.nudge: One is integer-valued; the other is measured on a continuous time scale.

scenes.title: Definition and assumptions
scenes.objective: State the homogeneous Poisson process properties.

blocks.body: N(t) is the number of events in (0,t], with N(0)=0 and nondecreasing integer-valued paths.
Counts in disjoint intervals are independent, and the distribution of an increment depends only on the interval length (stationary increments).

ask.q: What two properties distinguish increments of a homogeneous Poisson process?
ask.nudge: Consider disjoint intervals and shifting an interval without changing its length.

scenes.objective: Use the complement rule for a Poisson count.
scenes.problem: A machine fails according to a Poisson process at rate 0.2 per day. Find the probability of at least one failure in 3 days.

steps.why: The count over three days is Poisson with parameter 0.6.
It is easier to calculate zero failures.
The n=0 term of the Poisson law is e^(−λt).

scenes.title: Inter-arrival times are exponential
scenes.objective: Derive the distribution of the time to the first event.

blocks.body: T₁ is the time from time zero to the first event.

ask.q: Why is the first waiting time exponential?
ask.nudge: The event T₁>t means that no event has occurred by time t.

scenes.title: Guided problem: a waiting-time probability
scenes.objective: Calculate an exponential waiting-time probability with diminishing hints.
scenes.problem: Events arrive at rate 6 per hour. Find the probability that the wait for the next event exceeds 10 minutes.
hints: Convert 10 minutes to hours, or convert the rate to events per minute.
Use P(T₁>t)=e^(−λt), not the Poisson formula for an exact count.

solution.say: The first waiting time is Exp(6) when time is measured in hours.

scenario.title: Waiting for the next bus
body: Suppose arrivals at a stop are modelled by a homogeneous Poisson process with rate 6 buses per hour. The waiting time from the observation start to the next arrival has an exponential distribution with rate 6 per hour.
Ten minutes is one-sixth of an hour. The chance of waiting longer than ten minutes is the survival probability e^(−6×1/6), approximately 0.3679.
This probability is not the probability of exactly one bus in ten minutes. That latter question would use the Poisson count distribution.
scenario.q: What probability would you use for a wait longer than ten minutes?
scenario.answer: Use the exponential survival probability e^(−λt)=e^(−1), approximately 0.3679.

ask.q: What is the most common unit mistake in this problem?
ask.nudge: The rate is per hour, so express t in hours.

scenes.title: The kth arrival: Gamma and Erlang
scenes.objective: Relate successive exponential gaps to the time of the kth event.

blocks.body: Let X₁,X₂,… be the times between consecutive events. In a homogeneous Poisson process they are iid Exp(λ).
T_k=X₁+⋯+X_k~Gamma(shape k, rate λ), also called Erlang when k is a positive integer.
P(T_k>t)=P(N(t)≤k−1). The kth event has not occurred by t exactly when at most k−1 events have occurred.

ask.q: What distribution describes the time to the third event?
ask.nudge: It is the sum of three independent exponential inter-arrival times.

scenes.title: Worked example: time to the second event
scenes.objective: Calculate a kth-arrival probability using a Poisson count identity.
scenes.problem: Events occur at rate 2 per hour. Find the probability that the second event occurs after 1 hour.

steps.why: The second event has not occurred by one hour if there are zero or one events.
The count in one hour is Poisson(2).

steps.say: Add the zero- and one-count probabilities.
steps.why: Use the Poisson probabilities for n=0 and n=1.
This is the survival probability of the second arrival time.

scenes.intro: Mark each claim true or false, then compare the reason.

items.claim: The number of events in time t has a Poisson distribution with mean λt.
items.why: This is the defining count law of a homogeneous Poisson process.

items.claim: The mean inter-arrival time is λ.
items.why: The mean is 1/λ; λ is the event rate.

items.claim: The time to the third event is exponential with rate λ.
items.why: It is the sum of three iid exponential gaps, hence Gamma/Erlang.

items.claim: Counts in two disjoint intervals are independent.

items.why: Waiting longer than t is equivalent to observing no event by t.

ask.q: Which phrase should immediately make you think of a Gamma/Erlang distribution?

scenes.title: Guided problem: waiting for the third event
scenes.objective: Translate a kth-arrival probability into a Poisson count.
scenes.problem: A homogeneous Poisson process has rate 2 events per minute. Find P(T₃>1 minute), the probability that the third event has not occurred by one minute.
hints: Translate the event: T₃>1 means fewer than three events have occurred by time 1.
Use N(1)~Poisson(2), so add the probabilities for counts 0, 1 and 2.
Substitute into e^(−2)Σₙ₌₀²2ⁿ/n!. Keep the time unit in minutes.

solution.say: The event T₃>1 is equivalent to N(1)≤2: the third arrival has not yet occurred exactly when no more than two arrivals have occurred.
The count in one minute is Poisson with mean λt=2×1=2.

scenes.title: Summary: counts, gaps and arrival epochs
scenes.objective: Connect the main Poisson-process formulas before mastery practice.
body: For a homogeneous Poisson process, N(t)~Poisson(λt), so P(N(t)=n)=e^(−λt)(λt)^n/n!. Its mean and variance are both λt.
Counts in disjoint intervals are independent, and the distribution of an increment depends only on the interval length.
Inter-arrival times are iid Exp(λ), with survival e^(−λt), mean 1/λ and variance 1/λ².
The time T_k to the kth event is Gamma/Erlang(k,λ), with mean k/λ and variance k/λ².
Use P(T_k>t)=P(N(t)≤k−1) to switch between waiting-time and count questions. Convert units before substituting.

ask.q: A question asks for the probability that the fourth arrival occurs after time t. Which count event is equivalent?
ask.nudge: The fourth arrival is still pending when at most three events have occurred.
